QBI DEDUCTION CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What's your Section 199A qualified business income deduction worth?

Eligible owners of a sole proprietorship, partnership, S corporation, trust, or estate can deduct up to 20% of qualified business income (QBI) — but above a taxable-income threshold, a specified service business phases toward $0 and any other business is capped by its W-2 wages and UBIA of qualified property. This estimates the deduction for one qualified trade or business, including the 2026 rule changes.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Running an S-corp and setting your own W-2 salary? A lower salary raises this deduction (wages reduce QBI) but can also raise your audit risk — see the S-corp reasonable compensation calculator for that side of the same pass-through income.

1. Tax year, filing status & income

"Taxable income" here is your Form 1040 taxable income before this deduction is subtracted — the threshold test and the overall cap both use that figure. Net capital gain is net long-term capital gain plus qualified dividends; it reduces the amount the overall 20% cap is measured against, so leave it at $0 if you have neither.

2. Your qualified trade or business

One business. If you have QBI from more than one trade or business, or any of them reports a loss, see "What this does not cover" below before combining them here.

UBIA is the unadjusted basis immediately after acquisition of tangible depreciable property still within its depreciable period — usually equipment, machinery, or real property, not accumulated depreciation. Leave W-2 wages and UBIA at $0 if your taxable income is below the threshold above: neither field affects the deduction there.

3. REIT dividends & PTP income (optional)

This component gets 20% with no wage/UBIA limit and no SSTB reduction, ever — leave it at $0 if it doesn't apply to you.

Fill in your income and business details above, then click Calculate.

What this does not cover

  • One business only. Combining QBI, W-2 wages, and UBIA across more than one qualified trade or business — including netting a loss from one business against QBI from another, which the regulations require before applying the wage/UBIA limit — is not modeled here. Treat this as a single-business estimate.
  • Not a full tax return. This estimates one deduction only — not your total tax liability, self-employment tax, other deductions or credits, or state tax (most states either do not conform to this deduction or apply their own rules).
  • SSTB classification is confirmed by you, not verified against the statute and regulations here — check IRS Form 8995-A instructions and Treas. Reg. 1.199A-5 before relying on it.
  • The $400 minimum deduction (2026+) is modeled as a floor on the QBI-based amount before the overall taxable-income cap — a simplification for an edge case the statute's interaction with that cap does not fully spell out in plain guidance yet.

Common questions

What is the QBI deduction?

The Section 199A qualified business income deduction lets eligible owners of a sole proprietorship, partnership, S corporation, trust, or estate deduct up to 20% of their qualified business income (QBI) from that trade or business, plus 20% of qualified REIT dividends and publicly traded partnership (PTP) income. It does not apply to C corporations, and it is a deduction from taxable income, not a credit.

What is the taxable-income threshold, and what happens above it?

For 2025, the threshold is $191,950 (single, head of household, or married filing separately) or $383,900 (married filing jointly), with a phase-in range of $50,000 / $100,000 above that. For 2026, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act raised the threshold to $201,750 / $403,500 and widened the range to $75,000 / $150,000. Below the threshold, the deduction is simply 20% of QBI. Within the range, a specified service business's deduction phases toward $0 and a non-specified business's deduction phases toward the W-2 wage / UBIA limit. Above the top of the range, those limits apply in full.

What is a specified service trade or business (SSTB)?

Fields specifically listed in the statute and regulations: health, law, accounting, actuarial science, performing arts, consulting, athletics, financial services, brokerage services, investing and investment management, trading, dealing in securities/partnership interests/commodities, or any business where the principal asset is the reputation or skill of one or more employees or owners. Above the top of the phase-in range, an SSTB's QBI deduction from that business is $0 -- other qualified trades or businesses are unaffected.

What is the W-2 wage / UBIA limit?

Above the phase-in range, a non-SSTB's QBI deduction from a business is capped at the greater of 50% of the W-2 wages that business paid, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of the unadjusted basis immediately after acquisition (UBIA) of its qualified depreciable property. Within the phase-in range, the cap blends proportionally between no limit at all and this full limit.

What is the $400 minimum deduction, and when does it apply?

Starting tax year 2026 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a filer with at least $1,000 of qualified business income from an active qualified trade or business can claim at least a $400 QBI deduction, even if the phase-out or wage/UBIA formula would otherwise produce less. It does not apply for tax year 2025.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published statutory formula for ONE qualified trade or business to the numbers you enter. It does not model combining multiple businesses (including netting a loss from one against QBI from another), REIT/PTP income aside, and it is not a full tax return. Verify against the IRS's own guidance (Form 8995-A instructions) or a qualified tax professional before filing.

This calculator vs. the Form 8995-A worksheet by hand

The QBI deduction is arithmetic anyone can do with the IRS's own worksheet. The problem is that the worksheet has a few steps whose order matters, and a quick by-hand pass tends to apply a limit before or after it actually belongs.

Where a hand calculation usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Below the taxable-income thresholdApplies the SSTB phase-out or the W-2 wage/UBIA limit anyway, even though neither applies until taxable income clears the threshold for the filing status.Checks the threshold first and returns the unreduced 20% of QBI when income is below it, regardless of wages or UBIA.
SSTB inside the phase-in rangeApplies the wage/UBIA limit to the full W-2 wages and UBIA, then caps the result at $0 near the top of the range.Scales QBI, W-2 wages, AND UBIA by the same "applicable percentage" first, and only then computes 20% and the wage/UBIA test on the scaled-down figures.
The overall capStops at the QBI-based amount and never checks the second, independent limit.Also computes 20% of (taxable income minus net capital gain) and takes the lesser of the two, every time.
A business with negative QBITreats it as simply $0 and forgets it, or nets it against other income incorrectly.Reports $0 for that business this year and flags that the loss carries forward to reduce next year's QBI from the same business.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the most common mistake with the taxable-income threshold?

Applying the SSTB phase-out or the W-2 wage/UBIA limit at all when taxable income is still below the threshold for the filing status. Below threshold, the deduction is simply 20% of QBI -- neither limit applies yet, regardless of how low W-2 wages or UBIA are.

What's the most common mistake with the SSTB phase-out inside the range?

Applying the wage/UBIA limit to the FULL W-2 wages and UBIA figures, then just capping the result at $0 at the top of the range. Inside the phase-in range, an SSTB must first scale QBI, W-2 wages, AND UBIA by the same 'applicable percentage' -- and only then apply the 20% and the wage/UBIA test to the scaled-down figures.

What's the most common mistake with the overall cap?

Stopping at the QBI-based amount and never checking the second, independent limit: 20% of taxable income minus net capital gain. On a return with a low taxable income relative to QBI -- for example after large itemized deductions -- this second cap can bind well below what the QBI formula alone would allow.

What's the most common mistake with a business that lost money?

Treating negative QBI from one business as a $0 deduction and stopping there. It is $0 for THAT business this year, but the loss carries forward and reduces next year's QBI from the same business -- a step a quick by-hand estimate often drops entirely.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your full return, or how to combine more than one qualified trade or business. Both apply the same published federal formula to the numbers you enter for one business; verify against the IRS's own Form 8995-A instructions or a qualified tax professional before filing.

To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

why-is-my-qbi-deduction-0.html.text:
← back to the calculator

Why is my QBI deduction $0 (or much less than 20%)?

Twenty percent of qualified business income sounds like a number that should always be at least something. It is entirely possible for the actual deduction to be $0, or a small fraction of that 20% figure, and for that to be the statute working exactly as written rather than a mistake in a calculation. There are three distinct reasons this happens, and they call for different responses.

The three reasons a QBI deduction can be $0 (or near it)

ReasonWhat triggers itIs it really $0, or partial?
Specified service business (SSTB), above the phase-in rangeTaxable income is above the threshold-plus-range for your filing status, and the business is health, law, accounting, consulting, financial services, performing arts, athletics, or another field the statute names, or its principal asset is an owner's or employee's reputation or skill.Exactly $0 from that business. There is no floor -- the SSTB reduction reaches 100% at the top of the range and does not partially apply above it.
W-2 wage / UBIA limit, no SSTBTaxable income is above the threshold-plus-range, the business is not an SSTB, and it paid little or no W-2 wages and holds little or no depreciable qualified property (UBIA).Capped at the greater of 50% of wages or 25% of wages plus 2.5% of UBIA -- both near $0 if wages and UBIA are near $0, even though 20% of QBI itself might be large.
Negative QBIThe business's qualified business income for the year is negative -- possible even in a year with positive cash flow, once startup costs, Section 179, or a loss year's ordinary business deductions are counted.$0 for this business this year. The negative amount carries forward and reduces next year's QBI from the same business instead.

Common questions

Why did my specified service business's QBI deduction go to $0?

Above the top of the taxable-income phase-in range for your filing status, a specified service trade or business (SSTB) -- health, law, accounting, consulting, financial services, performing arts, athletics, or a business whose principal asset is an owner's or employee's reputation or skill -- gets $0 of QBI deduction from that business, full stop. There is no partial amount above the range; the SSTB reduction reaches 100% exactly at the top of the range and stays there.

My business isn't an SSTB. Why is my deduction still close to $0?

Above the phase-in range, a non-SSTB's deduction from a business is capped at the greater of 50% of that business's W-2 wages, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of the UBIA of its qualified property. A sole proprietor with no employees and no significant depreciable equipment can have both figures at or near $0, which caps the deduction at or near $0 even though the business is not an SSTB and 20% of QBI would otherwise be a large number.

Why is my deduction $0 even though my business made money?

Check whether QBI itself, not the deduction, is negative. Qualified business income is not simply revenue -- it is the net amount of income, gain, deduction, and loss from the business, so a year with heavy startup costs, a large Section 179 deduction, or a bad stretch can produce negative QBI even when cash flow was positive. Negative QBI produces a $0 deduction for that business this year and instead reduces the QBI that same business reports next year.

Can the 2026 minimum deduction fix a $0 result?

Only in narrow cases, and only for 2026 and later. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's $400 minimum deduction requires at least $1,000 of QBI from an active qualified trade or business, and it is layered on top of the SSTB and wage/UBIA rules, not a replacement for them -- it raises a small positive result up to $400, it does not turn a $0 SSTB result above the range, or a $0 result from negative QBI, into something positive.

How do I tell which of these applies to me?

Run your numbers through the calculator this page links to. It reports which limitation applied -- SSTB fully phased out, wage/UBIA limit, negative QBI carryforward, or none -- as a labeled finding alongside the dollar result, rather than just a final number with no explanation of why it is small.
